summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was identified.

The legal baseline a trans visitor encounters is national. Same-sex marriage and full adoption have been legal since 2013, with France's first same-sex wedding performed on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect, and civil solidarity pacts available since 1999. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced the term sexual identity, itself protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

Legal gender recognition rests on a statute signed on 18 November 2016 and in force from 1 January 2017. It abolished the requirements of sex-reassignment surgery and forced sterilisation, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires an applicant to go before a court rather than undergo any medical intervention. Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees by the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each establishment improvises around that provision, whether through special units or isolation restricting contact with other inmates. The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty has stated that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison. First-person accounts in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, the incarceration of an Argentinian trans woman, and heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements. The same feature covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It was built on roughly forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights, including placement by birth sex, isolation, exposure during strip searches and overcrowding risks, and it records no marked improvement since the authority's 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. It recommends that the 2016 depathologising law be translated into prison regulations, and it explicitly extends its coverage to intersex and non-binary people.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.
tangentialFactors:
No finding specific to Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes is available in the source inventory, so the division was covered by the dedicated country dossier and identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately. The regional assessment therefore rests on the national framework alone.

The custodial findings are drawn from establishments across France rather than from any single facility: the 2021 inspections covered men's and women's prisons, a remand establishment and a central police station in five locations, and the referrals behind the opinion accumulated nationally over more than a decade. Individual cases such as the Lille detention of 2014 or the Tarbes placement of 2024 illustrate a pattern the inspectorate describes as structural, not isolated.

The CGLPL document relied on here is an unofficial English translation of the opinion of 25 May 2021. The BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 and the StreetPress account of 7 March 2017 are journalistic first-person testimony rather than official findings, though both are consistent with the inspectorate's conclusions.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must appear before a court; the procedure in force since 1 January 2017 requires no surgery, no sterilisation and no medical intervention of any kind, and the legislature expressly rejected an amendment demanding proof of treatment. The change was enacted by the law of 18 November 2016, approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016.

Gender-affirming treatment is funded through the national health scheme because transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity falls within Penal Code article 225-1 as amended on 18 November 2016, and homophobic hate speech is punishable by up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment.

For residents in detention, placement continues to follow the sex on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, with treatment varying between establishments. The CGLPL issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty alongside its opinion of 25 May 2021, and the Défenseur des droits has issued a framework decision on trans rights setting out guidance for service providers.

Partner recognition rests on the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013, with civil solidarity pacts available since 1999 and full adoption permitted from 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
No usable finding specific to Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes is available: the region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and the inventory records no regional detention, policing or documentation data. Whether any establishment within the region applies the CGLPL's 2021 guidance, or how trans detainees here are placed, is unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory does not document enforcement outcomes for the gender-identity provisions of Penal Code article 225-1, nor any regional statistics on complaints, prosecutions or service-provider guidance. The practical effect of the Défenseur des droits framework decision within the region is likewise not sourced.

Border practice is evidenced by a single first-person account from 2017; no official or recent data on document screening of trans travellers at French entry points appears in the inventory. The frequency and current handling of such checks remain unresolved.
